Problem 17. Crossing the fictional border network of Elm
Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.
Countries are represented by the fictional states Elm, Iris, Alder, Yarrow, Cedar, Harbor. Shared borders: Elm–Iris, Iris–Alder, Alder–Yarrow, Elm–Cedar, Cedar–Harbor, Harbor–Yarrow.
Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.
What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Elm to Yarrow? Is Iris necessarily crossed?

1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Elm to Yarrow. 3. Remove Iris and check whether Yarrow is still reachable from Elm. 4. It is still reachable, so Iris is not unavoidable.
3 border crossing(s); Iris is not unavoidable.

Problem 21. Reading a layered map legend (A1)
A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.
Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village.
A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so.
Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: forest, road? Explain by intersecting the clues.
1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['forest', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['A1', 'B1'].
Map reading often means intersecting clues rather than recognizing one symbol in isolation.
Set model; each cell has an attribute set; return cells whose set is a superset of the required set.
